summary:
Space Outpost: Mission Commander is an interactive browser-based STEM game designed for children ages 7-12 to explore the real engineering challenges of human spaceflight. Young players take command of three authentic NASA missions, such as Mars Outpost (Jezero Crater), Artemis Moon Base (Shackleton Crater), and Lunar Gateway, where they must manage limited daily solar power (kWh) and solve operational dilemmas across changing space-weather hazards.

Instead of passive reading, the simulator teaches kids that space exploration requires tough engineering trade-offs: boosting radiation shielding during a solar flare or dust storm means cutting energy from hydroponic crops or thermal heaters. By translating real NASA datasets (DONKI space weather, OSDR radiation limits, and Mars/Lunar telemetry) into visual cause-and-effect gameplay, our solution inspires the next generation of explorers with realistic STEM problem-solving skills.
details:
Space Outpost: Mission Commander is an interactive browser-based STEM game built to show kids ages 7-12 what it actually takes to keep astronauts alive in deep space. Instead of passively reading facts about planets, young players step into the role of a Mission Commander across three real NASA destinations: a Mars outpost at Jezero Crater, an Artemis base at the Moon’s Shackleton Crater, and the Lunar Gateway station in deep space orbit. In every round, players receive incoming telemetry alerts and have to make tough, realistic engineering choices – first picking between two operational protocols (like running high-pressure MOXIE oxygen cycles, clearing electrostatic regolith dust, or retreating to water-wall storm shelters), and then dividing a strictly limited daily solar power budget across Oxygen & Heaters, Radiation Shielding, and Hydroponic Food & Water systems.

What makes our project effective is that it teaches the golden rule of spaceflight engineering: every choice is a trade-off. Kids quickly realize they can never run every system at full power at the same time, so surviving an X-class solar flare or a planet-encircling dust storm means temporarily sacrificing crop growth or cabin warmth to keep the crew safe. To keep young learners engaged without overwhelming them with raw spreadsheets, we designed a live vector habitat scene that visually reacts to their decisions – the sky turns dusty amber during storms, radiation alerts flash red, and the magnetic shield dome glows brighter as you route more power to it. At the end of a mission, players earn a custom Commander Rank Badge tailored to their survival strategy, encouraging them to replay and master all three destinations.

We built the entire application from scratch in Visual Studio Code using clean, zero-dependency HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript, with custom inline SVG graphics for the planetary scenes. When designing the game, we focused heavily on accessibility and scientific honesty: we wanted it to load instantly on any school Chromebook or tablet without downloads or logins, while grounding every scenario in real NASA open datasets – including DONKI space weather alerts, OSDR radiation and plant-growth thresholds, and Mars/Lunar environmental telemetry from Curiosity, Perseverance, MRO, and LRO. By turning real NASA data into intuitive cause-and-effect gameplay, our goal is to spark genuine curiosity and build systems-thinking skills in the next generation of space explorers.

Developed by the Bulbashi team for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Note: Generative AI (LLM) tools were used to assist with HTML/CSS/JavaScript code prototyping and English text editing.
